# The letters

After stating its system in brief, the 1446 book explained the letters one
class at a time: the initial consonants, the vowels, the final consonants.
Each class was explained by the same method.

Part I stated gog's whole system in brief. This part then explains gog's
letters one class at a time, as the 1446 book did. The marks are the initial consonants:
the visible forms, such as a dot, a bar or a line. A mark draws nothing until a
position places it. The positions are the vowels: `x`, `y` and `z`.
Only [`edge`](../marks/edge.qmd) takes none of them: a [`layout`](../transforms.qmd#layout-a-graph-placed-from-an-edge-table) transform computes its positions
instead. Each position has a scale, which decides where a number, a category or
a date falls on its axis. The refining channels are the final
consonants: `color`, `size`, `shape`, `pattern`, `opacity`. Each is optional,
and when it is mapped to a column, it gets a legend that shows which value
each color, size, shape, pattern or opacity stands for.

Three channels belong to none of these classes: `group`, `label` and `play`. On
a `line`, `group` makes the same split as `color`: one line per category. But
every line is drawn alike, so `group` gets no legend. It separates the lines,
but nothing on the plot shows how. `label` gives each `text` mark the words it
draws, rather than refining the mark. `play` splits the rows into frames and
plays them in order, the way a facet splits them into panels. Its chapter is
in Part III, [The sentences](sentences.qmd).

The [Data](../data.qmd) chapter opens this part with the table every sentence
starts from, because nothing can be drawn until a table is named. [The book's
data](../book-data.qmd) follows, saying where this book's own tables come from
and how to load one in any of the four languages. Then come the letters
themselves. [Choosing a mark](../marks/index.qmd) opens them, and then each mark
has a chapter of its own, fourteen in a row from [point](../marks/point.qmd) to
[edge](../marks/edge.qmd). After the marks, the [Scales](../scales.qmd) chapter
covers the scales of the positions `x`, `y` and `z`, and the [Channels and
legends](../channels.qmd) chapter covers the final consonants and their
legends. The [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) chapter shows the difference
between a column you *map* and a constant you *set*. The
[Transforms](../transforms.qmd) chapter closes the part: a transform derives new
values from your columns, such as counts, means or a smooth curve. Transforms
take more practice than any other kind of word. They are also what let you ask
questions of a table instead of only drawing it. The better you know them, the
better you can use gog, so read that chapter without hurrying.

Every mark chapter follows the same template, just as the 1446 book explained
each letter class by the same method. It says what the mark draws, what it
requires, what refines it and which transforms it takes. It then closes with
three sections that have the same names in every chapter: *What you can set*,
*What it refuses* and *What comes next*. A short summary, *In short*, may come
between the last two. That sameness is deliberate: it is the [No
Exceptions](../design-laws.qmd#law-2-no-exceptions) law applied to this book's structure. Learning
the second mark is faster than learning the first. By the fifth you know which
section answers which question, and you can read only the one you need.
